h: Royal births, prisoners of war and the Tattoo
p: The Royal Palace is where Mary, Queen of Scots gave birth to the future James VI in 1566, the king who would go on to unite the crowns of Scotland and England. The room is surprisingly small, which makes the moment feel all the more human. Next door, the Great Hall, built for James IV in the early 1500s, has a magnificent hammerbeam roof and walls bristling with weapons and armour.

Down in the vaults beneath the Great Hall, the Prisons of War exhibition recreates the cramped quarters where captured sailors and soldiers, including Americans during the War of Independence, were held. You can still see graffiti they carved into the old wooden doors, and it's one of the most atmospheric corners of the whole castle. Outside, look for the small cemetery for soldiers' dogs, a touching little spot many people miss.

There's a lot to take in, so allow at least two to three hours. The castle also holds the National War Museum and regimental museums, so if military history is your thing you could stay much longer. Arriving early in the day tends to be calmer, and timed tickets help you avoid disappointment in the busy months.

In August, the Esplanade transforms into the arena for the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, with grandstands, massed pipes and drums and a spectacular backdrop. At the top of the Royal Mile, just below the castle, you'll find Camera Obscura and World of Illusions for a fun change of pace, while Princes Street Gardens sit far below the castle rock for a picnic with a view.
